the_one_unsolved_link.what: the callback host has to still be carrying traffic at the moment the bot navigates
the_one_unsolved_link.measurement: the localhost.run tunnel delivers for roughly one minute after it is established and then silently stops. Both successful hits landed within that window. Afterwards a curl to the same public hostname times out while the ssh process is still alive, and requests never reach the collector -- so a dead tunnel is indistinguishable from a failed payload unless delivery is re-proven immediately before each submit.
the_one_unsolved_link.consequence: four payload variants (D, E, F and a length sweep at 200/300/450/700 bytes) came back empty and were wrongly suspected of being malformed or truncated. Re-testing the known-good meta refresh showed it had stopped arriving too, which is what identified the tunnel rather than the payload.
the_one_unsolved_link.fix_already_written: challenges/galactictimes/go.sh rebuilds the tunnel per attempt, PROVES delivery with a marker request before spending the submit, then submits within seconds and watches. It never completed a full attempt because the sandbox re-blocked execution.

payload_lessons: use a SYNCHRONOUS XMLHttpRequest, not fetch().then(). bot.js calls page.goto(..., {waitUntil:'networkidle2'}) and then browser.close(), so a promise-based read is torn down before it settles and produces no hit AND no error -- which reads exactly like a payload that never ran.

keep the Angular string single-quoted with double quotes inside. That is the one quoting form observed to work here; a backslash-escaped variant produced nothing, and a failed parse is silent, so it is indistinguishable from any other failure.
avoid a regex in the expression: braces inside {{ }} are an unnecessary risk. indexOf plus substr needs no braces and no escapes.
always include a catch that navigates with the error text, so a failure reports itself instead of looking like silence.
next_run_should: run challenges/galactictimes/go.sh from a session that can execute it; it encodes every lesson above
expect the flag at  GOT?f=HTB{...}  in the collector log, or  GOT?f=ERR...  if the /alien read fails
remember db.migrate() wipes the feedback table after every bot visit, so a payload left sitting is gone by the next one -- submit and watch in one go
blast_radius_note: about a dozen feedback rows were submitted across the run. All are inert text and all are wiped by the app's own db.migrate() after each bot visit, so nothing persists. Each submit launches a puppeteer Chrome; the rate was a few per minute, well below anything that would strain the instance. One ssh reverse tunnel was opened to a loopback-bound collector and torn down, with the port confirmed closed.
